speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) whether he will consider delaying the wider roll-out of the ERP 2.0 On-Board Unit (OBU) for cars to address users’ feedback; (b) if so, how will the Ministry ensure a user-centric approach that incorporates users’ concerns while avoiding a complete system reversal; and (c) how will users’ experiences be prioritised during the development and implementation of new technologies related to a ERP system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: asked the Minister for Transport with the implementation of ERP 2.0 which involves the relocation of the processing unit carrying CEPAS (Specification for Contactless e-Purse Application) or NETS cards to the front passenger footwells or other technically feasible positions in motor vehicles, whether it can be made mandatory for all carpark operators to upgrade their systems so that it will no longer be necessary for drivers to tap their cards at carpark terminal stations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Its replacement, ERP 2.0, is based on Global Navigation Satellite System technology.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is able to perform all the functions of the current ERP system, plus additional capabilities to better manage traffic flow on our roads, without the need for physical gantries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I mentioned during the Ministry of Transport (MOT) Committee of Supply (COS) debate earlier this year, it also provides the option for distance-based charging in future, which could allow for a one-off increase in our total vehicle population while keeping traffic congestion in check.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The transition from the current in-vehicle unit to the on-board unit (OBU) is a major exercise involving many motorists and a diverse range of vehicles, vehicle makes and models, including new and existing vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The process will take a few years to complete.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Before embarking on the installation exercise, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) worked with the dealers to study how the OBU could be best installed in different vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA has staged out the installation exercise, starting with a group of early adopters since August 2023.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Of these, around 11,000 are fleet vehicles, including buses and company-registered vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This phased approach gives the workshops time to prepare their workers and progressively ramp up their resources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It also allows LTA to take in feedback from stakeholders and understand the areas for improvement, before extending to other vehicles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some may choose to have the touch-screen display, while others may prefer to use their in-vehicle display or their mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our recommendation is to install the touch-screen display, I have done so for my car, but this is a choice for the vehicle owner to make.
The vehicle owner can also choose where to place the touch-screen display subject to technical feasibility, for example, on the driver side or in the middle of the dashboard.
If a vehicle owner decides not to install the touch-screen display, a unit of the display will still be given to him, so that he has the option to install it subsequently if he changes his mind.
Likewise, the vehicle owner can decide where to place the processing unit.
For the initial phase of installation, LTA only allowed the processing unit to be installed on the passenger side.
Service ambassadors will also be present at the showrooms and workshops to explain the options to vehicle owners before OBU installation.
By providing more choices, the process becomes more complex and the workshops will require more time to complete the installation.
However, we think the trade-off is necessary, to allow vehicle owners to have the flexibility to customise their preferred options and not have a "one-size-fits-all" approach.
We understand the concerns from early adopters on the inconvenience of having to remove and reinsert the CEPAS (Specification for Contactless e-Purse Application) card in the processing unit.
This is a key design feature of the OBU.
You do not need to remove the CEPAS card from the processing unit when you are driving the vehicle.
For example, LTA has implemented a button on the touch-screen display to deactivate the card when motorists want to use their complimentary parking tickets.
They can press the button on the touch-screen display.
The card will be deactivated and they can then use their complimentary ticket to exit the carpark.
If the motorist forgets to reactivate the card after leaving the carpark, the correct amount will still be deducted from the card balance when he reaches the next active ERP gantry.
This is unlike the current in-vehicle unit (IU).

If the motorist pulls out the card from the IU to use his complimentary parking ticket and forgets to re-insert it – it happens to us sometimes – he will not be able to make ERP payment when his vehicle passes through an active ERP gantry.
Another scenario is the topping-up of the CEPAS card.
Today, some of us may reach the carpark gantry only to realise that our balance is low, we must then find a way to exit the queue to top-up the card.
With the OBU, your CEPAS card balance will be shown once you start the car.
This can help remind motorists to top-up before reaching the gantry.
For added convenience, motorists can sign up for auto top-up so they need not manually top up their card when the balance is low.
LTA will deploy service ambassadors to workshops to guide motorists who wish to sign up for automatic top-up of their CEPAS card when they install the OBU.
The third scenario where removal of the CEPAS card may be needed, is at certain carparks which require motorists to tap their cards at carpark terminal stations, as Mr Murali asked.
There are, however, some privately-owned carparks which have yet to implement EPS.
We welcome the initiative from NETS to provide a complimentary One Motoring Card for motorists who install the OBU.
Motorists can use this additional card at the privately-owned carparks without EPS, without having to remove their CEPAS card from the processing unit.
This is not the main reason for doing ERP 2.0, but the added capabilities provide opportunities for LTA and its partners to offer some features that could help enhance user safety.
It will include not just the fixed cameras, but also red light and mobile cameras used by the Traffic Police to enforce against speeding.
LTA will continue to take in feedback from motorists and develop features that can help enhance safety and convenience for motorists.
These additional features can be pushed out to motorists "over-the-air", after the OBUs have been installed.
Motorists do not need to bring their vehicles to the workshop for these software upgrades.
We appreciate the feedback from our early adopters, which LTA has taken on board where feasible and made improvements to enhance user choice, user convenience and user safety.
LTA will continue to gather feedback from motorists, workshops and dealers to further enhance the user experience for all motorists, as we proceed with the installation exercise.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Actually, he has answered my last supplementary question.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some have also been asking, since the motorcycle OBU is smaller, can that be used for cars as well, rather than having the bigger units for the cars.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, if there is none, then, why not?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If yes, then continue to do so, so that we can get more feedback from the motorists, and we can improve upon it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The third supplementary question was to ask the Minister whether his car has been fitted with the OBU, but the Minister had answered yes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I would like to find out from the Minister's personal experience using this and then what are the difficulties that he has encountered?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, the point about the installation at the driver's footwell.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, as some of the mechanics have shared and as it was reported in the CNA article that Dr Lim mentioned, it is not so straightforward for all vehicle makes and models.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because depending on the design and the layout and the specifications of different vehicles, the preferred location, the ideal location, may vary from vehicle to vehicle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the trade-off between giving more choices to vehicle owners is that it does introduce more complexity to the installation process.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we think this trade-off is important because we do need to respect the individual choices of vehicle owners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It does not mean that every vehicle can install the processing unit at the driver's footwell.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It depends on the layout and design of the vehicle, but in many vehicle types, this is possible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we do want to provide this option, even though it is not always possible, to the vehicle owners so that for those who prefer to have it closer to them, they have that option that they can choose.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But this process is best done in discussion with the service ambassadors and the mechanics at the workshops so that the vehicle owners understand what are the trade-offs, what are the options, before the OBU installation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, even if you do not sign up for auto top-up and you need to manually remove and do a manual top-up, you can do that after the car is parked.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You do not need to do it while you are in the driver's seat, while you are driving.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when you are driving, you do not need to remove the card from the processing unit.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is why we introduced some of these additional features to make it such that you do not need to remove the card while you are driving, for safety and for convenience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It takes a few years, involving different workshops, different vehicle makes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I just want to register my appreciation to our partners from the industry, the workshops, the motor dealers, our mechanics and also our staff and our partners who are serving as service ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is a lot of hard work for them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They have to engage the vehicle owners, explain the options to them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I think this is an important part of the overall installation process – so that people are clear what are their options, so that when they go in and they choose a certain configuration, they understand what are the trade-offs, what are the pros and cons.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Dr Lim also asked about the one-piece OBU, which is for the motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you think about the physics of it: in an enclosed environment with glass, it is like a greenhouse.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You do have a greenhouse effect, which will cause the interior of the car, in an enclosed space, to be warmer.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I just read one article from AsiaOne and I think they also did their own measurements.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And it is quite clear from all the various measurements that we have done, that the footwell, whether passenger side or driver side, the temperature there is significantly lower than the temperature on the dashboard during a hot sunny day.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the ambient temperature, if it is about 35 degrees, for the motorcycle it is pretty much that, because it is not an enclosed space.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And then it will affect the functionality of this unit.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You could design it such that there is cooling, there is a fan inside, but that will make it very bulky and I do not think motorists will want a very big and bulky one-piece unit on their dashboard.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: By splitting it up, we give motorists the option of deciding whether or not you want the display, because it is not part of the same piece; you can choose, it is optional.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And you can also choose where to put your processing unit.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In some vehicle makes, the dealer actually recommended that one of the options available is that you can also put it below the driver's seat, if you prefer not to see it.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And because we have now designed the process such that you do not need to remove your card while you are driving, actually that option is now possible, viable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will not cause inconvenience to the driver and if that is what the drivers prefer, they have that option to choose from.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think I mentioned in my main reply, we will continue to gather feedback from motorists, from the mechanics at the workshops, from our service ambassadors for how we can further improve the user experience, how we can further improve our communications.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And lastly, Dr Lim asked me about my own experience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why, I was very happy when LTA developed that feature where I could just deactivate the card by pressing a button on the touch-screen display.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I can do that very conveniently now; I do not have to take my card in and out.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are also other features that we have given feedback to LTA from the group of early adopters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think that is a continuous process for improvement and I want to thank our early adopters as well, for their inputs, for their feedback, and if amongst them, any of the early adopters feel that they now want to switch their configuration.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I see three more Members who want to ask supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I repeat my earlier reminders: for those asking, keep your supplementary questions short; and likewise, for those responding, keep your replies short.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And limit it to one supplementary question, please.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is the Minister prepared to order a system redesign of the ERP 2.0 to make it mobile first?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And to be clear, I do not mean providing the mobile phone as an as a secondary option, like what the Minister had just said.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am talking about making it a default option.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And secondly, I understand that there are no immediate plans to implement distance-based charging, but given that distance-based charging is one of the key reasons for this new system – its implementation seems inevitable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My question is, has the Government considered the significant cost impact that distance-based charging will have on those who drive for a living, including taxi drivers, private hire drivers, and delivery drivers and riders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I have said in my COS speech that we are looking at distance-based charging as a possible option that we need to study further.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In my COS speech, I also acknowledge that there are trade-offs affecting different groups of stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Therefore, we need to be quite careful and deliberate in how we go about with this review.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think that in my main reply, I did not suggest anything that this is an inevitable outcome, as what Mr Giam mentioned.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I will urge Mr Giam not to overstate the point.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It depends on what you want to use a smartphone for.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you want to use a smartphone for displaying the information, we are allowing that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is not something that would be unworkable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have studied that option, and we are going to allow people to opt out of the display and to use a smartphone or their in-vehicle display, if they wish to.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, because your smartphone is something that you carry with you.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We need, for the purposes of ERP – whether it is distance-based or other types of usage-based charging – you need a device that is secured to the vehicle so that you know where the vehicle is and there is no dispute about whether the device is functioning or not.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is also a second consideration, Sir, which is the security of the data transmission.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because the OBU is designed to transmit the information one-way, whereas a phone, you would have two-way transmission.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But certainly, I think as part of integrating with the processing unit and the antenna, the use of a smartphone to replace the touch-screen display is a possibility.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are only at Question No 8, so I will allow one last supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, not just to look at the temperature, that is one factor, but also to take into account safety aspects.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, for example, if there is going to be an accident, we did crash tests as well, to make sure that the OBU, if it is installed properly, according to the proper procedure, will not pose a safety risk to the motorist and passenger.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is quite a comprehensive set of tests that has been done to take care of the different aspects, but what we need to continue to do is to work with our partners and with stakeholders, including motorists, mechanics, our service ambassadors, to continue to find ways in which we can improve the user experience and allow more value to be delivered to motorists with this capabilities of the ERP 2.0 system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond what I have shared earlier, there could be more functionalities that could be possible and we remain open to good ideas from our stakeholders on how we can maximise this value for motorists, through the capabilities and functionalities of ERP 2.0.
